video.title: How Shoulder Rotation Syncs Your Contact

classification.reason: The coach analyzes pro footage (Swiatek, Federer, Alcaraz, Sinner, Djokovic, Nadal, Dimitrov, Kyrgios) to teach the mechanical principle of syncing contact point with shoulder internal rotation.

problem.title_as_question: How Does Shoulder Rotation Sync Your Forehand Contact Point?
problem.definition: Players struggle with erratic contact and inconsistent string angles when their contact point does not match the precise moment their shoulder initiates internal rotation.
prerequisites: awareness of shoulder internal and external rotation

symptoms.description: The racket face is excessively closed at contact, causing the ball to be buried straight into the net or ground.
Contact feels uncomfortable, jammed, or painful when forcing the strike location.

causes.statement: Every effortless forehand must make contact right at the exact onset of internal shoulder rotation as it switches from back-roll to forward-roll.
Allowing the shoulder to turn over too far before contact destroys the string angle and forces the ball downward.
Players try to imitate a generic or pro contact point rather than matching contact to their individual anatomical release point.

angles.summary: The humerus transitions from maximum external rotation to forward internal roll, and contact must coincide with the start of this transition.
Swiatek releases early with a bent elbow closer to the body, whereas Federer and Dimitrov hold external rotation much longer and release way out in front.
Players can intuitively sense when the shoulder stops stretching and releases forward without calculating millisecond timing windows.
Believing that there is one universal objective contact point causes players to force their strike out front and close the racket face.

solutions.summary: Take a comfortable, painless pressing swing and identify the exact spatial location where your shoulder has just started turning over.
Feel for the exact moment the shoulder stops stretching and releases forward, and hit through that sensation.
Align contact with where your shoulder naturally releases rather than copying an exaggerated contact point far in front.
